sentences.text: Santanadactylus is described as a rather large pterosaur, with Peter Wellnhofer indicating a wingspan between 2.9 and 5.7 meters for the various species.
Paul de Buisonjé estimated the wingspan of the type species S. brasilensis to be 6 meters, a figure that exceeds the range given by Wellnhofer.
The preserved skull section of S. araripensis showed no crest, distinguishing it from other large pterosaurs of the time.
The animal may have been adapted for gliding rather than flapping flight, suggesting a specific mode of locomotion.
The genus Santanadactylus was named by the Dutch paleontologist Paul de Buisonjé in 1980, with the type species being S. brasilensis, a name referring to Brazil.
The holotype UvA M 4894 consists of the upper right humerus, right scapula, and coracoid, housed at the Geological Institute of the University of Amsterdam.
The species S. spixi was intermediate in size compared to the other species named by Wellnhofer.
Wellnhofer indicated that the wingspan of various Santanadactylus species ranged from 2.9 to 5.7 meters.
De Buisonjé first assigned Santanadactylus to the family Criorhynchidae, a concept that is no longer used.
Wellnhofer considered it a member of the Ornithocheiridae, but the parent group and family of Santanadactylus is now considered to be Pteranodontidae.
Bennett (1989) assigned the holotype of S. brasilensis to the family Pteranodontidae, according to his own definition of that group.
Fossils of Santanadactylus have been found in the Albian-aged Romualdo Member of the Santana Formation in the Araripe Plateau, Brazil.
It is debated whether the four named species of Santanadactylus belong to the same genus.
Thomas and McDavid (2025) suggested that the paratype RGM.631745 cannot be confidently referred to Santanadactylus because it belongs to Azhdarchomorpha.
Recent studies consider S. araripensis a dubious species.
Wellnhofer removed S. spixi from the genus in 1991.

Chris Bennett suggested that S. araripensis and S. pricei were pteranodontids. Chris Bennett suggested that S. spixi was a dsungaripterid. Unwin (2003) proposed that S. spixi was a species of Tupuxuara. Averianov (2014) considered S. spixi a nomen dubium likely synonymous with Tupuxuara longicristatus.
